essence: This ahnika takes up the remaining observance for the living.
Initiation, ending in śrāddha, is manifold — for purification, liberation, enjoyment, or both.
Initiation that purifies but does not directly free; intent-freed and direct with-seed initiations.
For the twice-initiated, lifelong conduct is taught — putrakas and the rest — to attain identity.
Whether craving enjoyment or liberation, credible through guru, scripture, own consciousness — the guru initiates to purify.
Purified, he knows the self by his own doctrine, then cultivates the practice for enjoyment or liberation.
Who holds enjoyment-liberation by faith in the Ācārya should be told the conduct that removes his obstacle.
Equal faith in own and guru's consciousness — the remaining observance is prescribed to end the obstacle.
One who renounces other-dependence and stands on his own, by faith or by Ācārya-faith alone.
The natural and the seedless both teach this remaining observance; progressive identity is guru-devotion.
For this purpose both constant and occasional practice are fixed; the optional is dropped, since desires vary.
Constant rule: the three junctures' observance — deity, vow, guru, fire, scripture, compassion to beings.
Occasional: festival worship and muttering, plus special pavitraka sequences.
Many types of Ācārya and initiation were examined; explanation follows to the occasional.
First the guru plainly teaches the constant rule to the disciple, having gauged his fitness.
Seeing fitness for the main and other mantras, he hands the root-mantra to that disciple.
The scripture-initiated, free of doubt, yet unfit for the main, serves by other practice.
For the sādhaka craving enjoyment, or the aspirant, the mantra is given by flower-fall to accomplish the aim.
In the far-spread, the qualified, or the rite — the guru, knowing his fitness, performs the rite in brief.
If a mantra-form is lacking, the guru writes it and teaches it, especially in the higher doctrine.
Mantras are syllable-natured or reflection-natured; the guru transfers his undivided consciousness into the disciple.
A written mantra is powerless by nature; imagined from convention, it gleams only from the book.
Book-learned vidyā is named in Siddha doctrine; the knower finds mantra-power even from a book.
Bhairavī's purification is natural; knowing the guru as supreme-bliss-revolving.
Having worshipped in such places, perform the rite; a disciple's practice is not known by another.
So the guru keeps secrecy; the defective is void; or the pure triple goddess, or one from the mate's union.
Speak one pure goddess or the mate-natured; the clear mantra is whispered from the guru's mouth.
Hearing the practice, he practices mentally; well-taught, the triad — place, body, inner purification.
Nyāsa, meditation, muttering, mudrā, worship — with effort; at dawn he recalls his former deity.
Having done the day's duty and grown pure, taking refuge north-facing in place, body, inner triad.
Purifying mantras, placing them rightly, mudrā, meditation on difference and non-difference.
In body, breath, intellect, ether, earth — worship by mind there; mutter and offer to the god by capacity.
To attain identity practice at each juncture; the four directions are for others.
The fourfold juncture is Tantric; we do not hold the variant; the time-chapter earlier declared it fourfold.
Having concentrated the juncture within, practice the rite — fourfold juncture, or one disciple.
Devoted to study, knowledge, guru-duty — the juncture-risen meditation yields endless identity.
By that purification, all time becomes identity; at the desired time worship with flowers, liquor and the rest.
On the altar the disciple works by capacity; well-purified, do the whole rite, inner muttering at the end.
Make the argha vessel from one's own dear mantra; sprinkle the altar and flowers with it.
Then intending door, seat, and guru-succession, worship Śiva absorbed in one's own body.
Seeing that altar as sky, crystal, pure consciousness, one sees the deity-group there.
By reflection, mirroring, and consciousness, this invocation is chief — like a fan of winds.
As wind is held by a fan, the all-going thing-doing mantra-circle arises.
By fifty-four this principle is stated; so in the Nirmaryāda teaching, spoken by the Lord.
The god is all-going, boundless — how is Śiva invoked? Thus the Lord was asked and answered.
By impression the goddess is invoked and dismissed; in the god's ultimate truth there is no invocation or dismissal.
Invoked by me, established on the altar, worshipped and praised and gladdened — then dismiss the god.
For unawakened beings, to generate satisfaction; otherwise how would invocation serve?
Know time as engaged in the Lord's rule; progressively god-attainment precedes the world.
The lamp of knowledge destroys all ignorance; whence is the god brought, or where led?
By gross and subtle difference, he abides everywhere; in the invoked, offer flowers and liquor.
Incense and libation by faith, devotion, fitting strength; by śakti's blaze and nāda, mantras with liquor by palas.
Red before the libation, flowers and incense after; do not libate a mantra that has not come.
He takes half the body, as Śambhu said; whatever blossoms in his mind he grants.
By that he worships, per Śambhu's decision; sādhakas craving enjoyment are bound by niyati.
The liberation-seeker who knows principles is unrestricted; he touches the special for a special cause.
Red cotton-wool like a seed-heap is enjoyment's; varied specials are stated by cause.
By place, time, quality, substance, action — a small act or one giving heart-delight.
By the external, born of imagination, or imagined agents; for the liberation-seeker no special rule serves the final good.
Not in Brahman are abundance, scantiness, bad states; essence is consciousness, its bliss-density.
Action aims at identity by giving heart-delight; Śiva's non-difference flows with that group's taste.
Offer that in the supreme abode for worship; in many hymns, as I spoke in my own ahnika.
Surpassing the supreme truth, radiance shines; worship that supreme nectar — knowers of the secret.
Support-bearing wonder-taste, sprinkling, moment-washed, taken by mind; flowers by nature, heart argha-vessel succession with the goddess.
Three worlds' various taste-essence: heart-cakra pressed upward, discrimination's weight squeezing out consciousness-nectar removing birth, age, death.
Contemplating the three verses' collected meaning, satisfy the deity-group by any means.
Exhibit mudrā after, mentally or by yoga, by speech, mantra-yoga, or body-placement.
Having muttered, hand all to the deity; that is the doership-principle's determination before the rite.
Then dismiss by applying consciousness-identity; or let the fire-abiding mantra be satisfied per procedure.
From door, seat, guru-group the offering is made; eat except others', then throw the deep water.
Water-born beings earlier initiated by Śambhu himself, by rite, by future, by Mīnanātha's incarnation.
Even the uninitiated cat, mouse and the rest are eaten; that gives doubt-anxiety, disease, hell.
Therefore the principle-knower destroys doubt-anxiety; openly he does not act for worldly gain.
In the Mata Mahā-śāstra the Lord himself said this, devoted to removing doubt-contraction.
Thus others' doubt will not shine in the mind; having washed and bathed with flowers, then worship.
All flowers standing there are thrown into the deep water; this altar-sacrifice is Śambhu's constant rite.

rasa.dominant: śānta (tranquility) with adbhuta weight (rest in the installed form; wonder at the rite)
rasa.justification: The ahnika teaches the remaining observance after initiation: constant and occasional rites, daily worship, invocation/dismissal, and the body as temple; tranquility rests in the installed form.

sections.SUMMARY: The ahnika teaches the śeṣavṛtti: the remaining observance after initiation — constant and occasional rites, daily worship, invocation and dismissal, and the body as temple.
sections.FUNCTION: Establishes śeṣavṛtti: the remaining observance after initiation — constant and occasional rites, daily worship, invocation and dismissal, and the body as temple.
